result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [DataScan.to_dict()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Pointblank description: Export the profile as a structured dictionary. twitter-card: title: >- [DataScan.to_dict()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Pointblank description: Export the profile as a structured dictionary. title: >- [DataScan.to_dict()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Export the profile as a structured dictionary. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Export the profile as a structured dictionary. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/blob/main/pointblank/datascan.py#L708-L790){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature DataScan.to_dict() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} A profile is worth keeping when it serves as a baseline: a record of what a table looked like at one point, to compare later scans against, or to store alongside the table in a catalog. `to_dict()` returns the whole profile as plain Python data, which [`from_dict()`](`pointblank.DataScan.from_dict`) turns back into a `DataScan`. For a JSON string or file, use [`to_json()`](`pointblank.DataScan.to_json`) or [`save_to_json()`](`pointblank.DataScan.save_to_json`). The profile includes the first five non-missing values of each column (`sample_data`). If the table holds sensitive values, keep that in mind before storing or sharing the result. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[str, Any]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A dictionary with two keys. `"metadata"` holds the table name, the row count, the list of column names, and `"skipped_columns"` (a dictionary mapping each column of an unsupported type to its type). `"columns"` holds a list with one entry per summarized column, each a dictionary with `"colname"`, `"coltype"`, `"sample_data"`, and `"statistics"` (a dictionary mapping each statistic's name to its value). ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Let's scan a small table of sensor readings, where one reading is missing. ::: {#28e424d3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pointblank as pb import polars as pl readings = pl.DataFrame( {"sensor": ["T1", "T2", "T3", "T4"], "temp_c": [21.4, 22.1, None, 20.8]} ) profile = pb.DataScan(readings, tbl_name="readings").to_dict() profile["metadata"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'table_name': 'readings', 'row_count': 4, 'columns': ['sensor', 'temp_c'], 'skipped_columns': {}} ``` ::: ::: Each column has its own entry, with the statistics in a nested dictionary: ::: {#8cd1193a .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} profile["columns"][1]["statistics"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {'n_missing': 1, 'n_unique': 4, 'mean': 21.433333333333334, 'median': 21.4, 'std': 0.6506407098647716, 'min': 20.8, 'max': 22.1, 'p05': 20.806, 'q_1': 21.1, 'q_3': 21.75, 'p95': 22.03, 'iqr': 0.6499999999999986} ``` ::: ::: The missing reading is counted in `n_missing` and left out of the other statistics. The statistics keep their Python types (the minimum and maximum of a date column, for example, are `datetime.date` values), and passing the dictionary to [`from_dict()`](`pointblank.DataScan.from_dict`) gives back the same profile.
